about: Original sentence-combining items (Grades 4–6) written for this platform: compound subjects and predicates, and/but/or/so, because/although/when, relative who/which. Loaded by the question seed only when this file is present.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence with a compound subject. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: The two sentences have the same predicate (plays football), so the two subjects are joined with and. Two people need the verb play, not plays.
explanation.tip: Find the words that repeat. Write them only once.

combine.hint: Who plays football? Put both names before the verb.
accepted: Omar and Khalid play football.
Khalid and Omar play football.

items.stem: Join the sentences into one sentence with a compound predicate (one subject that does more than one thing).

explanation.whyCorrect: Both sentences are about the falcon, so the subject is written once and the two actions are joined with and.
explanation.tip: Keep one subject and join the two actions.

sentences: The falcon flew over the dunes.
combine.hint: What did the falcon do? Two things.
accepted: The falcon spread its wings and flew over the dunes.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: But joins two complete sentences that show a surprise or a difference. A comma goes before but.
explanation.tip: Two complete sentences joined by but need a comma before but.

combine.hint: Is the second idea a surprise after the first one?
accepted: The soup was hot, but Lina ate it quickly.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: So joins a cause and its result. The rain is the cause and playing inside is the result. A comma goes before so.
explanation.tip: Cause first, then so, then the result.

combine.hint: Which sentence tells what happened because of the other one?
accepted: It started to rain, so we played inside.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Or joins two choices. With two complete sentences, put a comma before or; with one subject and two actions, no comma is needed.
explanation.tip: Or shows a choice between two things.

combine.hint: What are the two choices?
accepted: You can read a book, or you can draw a picture.
You can read a book or draw a picture.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Because tells the reason. The cold morning is the reason Sara wore a jacket. If because comes first, put a comma after the reason.
explanation.tip: Because comes right before the reason.

combine.hint: Why did Sara wear a jacket?
accepted: Sara wore a jacket because the morning was cold.
Because the morning was cold, Sara wore a jacket.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word to tell more about the noun.

explanation.whyCorrect: Who replaces he and tells more about my uncle. The who part goes right after the noun it describes.
explanation.tip: Who is used for people. Put it right after the person.

combine.hint: Which word does he stand for?
accepted: My uncle, who lives in Qassim, sells dates.
My uncle who lives in Qassim sells dates.

items.stem: Join the sentences into one sentence. Put the things that are the same in a list.

explanation.whyCorrect: The three sentences end the same way, so the three fruits become a list. Commas separate the items, and and comes before the last one.
explanation.tip: Use commas between the items in a list.

combine.hint: What is the same in all three sentences?
accepted: Apples, mangoes, and figs are sweet.
Apples, mangoes and figs are sweet.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: But shows a contrast: the museum was ready on time, the guide was not. A comma goes before but.
explanation.tip: A comma comes before but when it joins two sentences.

combine.hint: What is different between the two sentences?
accepted: The museum opened at nine, but the guide arrived late.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: So shows a result: he bought a bottle because he forgot his own. A comma goes before so.
explanation.tip: Cause, comma, so, result.

sentences: He bought one at the shop.
combine.hint: Which sentence is the result?
accepted: Fahad forgot his water bottle, so he bought one at the shop.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: When tells the time something happened. If the when part comes first, a comma follows it.
explanation.tip: When the time part comes first, end it with a comma.

combine.hint: What happened first?
accepted: When the bell rang, the students lined up.
The students lined up when the bell rang.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Although shows that the second idea is surprising: a long test, but she still finished early.
explanation.tip: Although goes before the idea that makes the other one surprising.

combine.hint: Which fact makes the other one surprising?
accepted: Although the test was long, Noura finished early.
Noura finished early although the test was long.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word to tell more about the noun.

explanation.whyCorrect: Which replaces the tent in the second sentence and tells more about it. Which is used for things and animals, not people.
explanation.tip: Which is used for things. Put it right after the thing it describes.

combine.hint: Which noun is repeated?
accepted: The camel carried the tent, which was very heavy.

items.stem: Join the sentences into one sentence with a compound predicate (one subject that does more than one thing).

explanation.whyCorrect: One subject (Reem) does three things, so the actions become a list with commas and and before the last action.
explanation.tip: Write the subject once, then list the actions.

combine.hint: How many things did Reem do?
accepted: Reem washed the dishes, dried them, and put them away.
Reem washed the dishes, dried them and put them away.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: But balances a problem and a reward. A comma comes before but because both parts are complete sentences.
explanation.tip: Two complete sentences joined by but need a comma.

sentences: The road to Abha is steep.
The view from the top is worth it.
combine.hint: What is the problem, and what makes it worth it?
accepted: The road to Abha is steep, but the view from the top is worth it.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Because introduces the reason for practising. Starting with because needs a comma after the reason.
explanation.tip: Because comes right before the reason.

sentences: They wanted to win the cup.
combine.hint: Why did the team practise?
accepted: The team practised every evening because they wanted to win the cup.
Because they wanted to win the cup, the team practised every evening.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word to tell more about the noun.

explanation.whyCorrect: Who replaces she and describes the scientist. The who part sits right after the scientist, inside the sentence.
explanation.tip: Put the who part right after the person it describes.

sentences: The scientist studied the coral reef.
combine.hint: Who is she?
accepted: The scientist who studied the coral reef won an award.
The scientist, who studied the coral reef, won an award.
The scientist, who won an award, studied the coral reef.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Although shows a contrast: you expect a crowded room to be noisy, but it stayed quiet.
explanation.tip: Although goes before the fact that makes the other one surprising.

combine.hint: What would you expect in a crowded room?
accepted: Although the library was crowded, it stayed quiet.
The library stayed quiet although it was crowded.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one sentence with a compound subject. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: The predicate (attended the ceremony) is the same, so the two subjects are joined with and into a compound subject.
explanation.tip: Write the repeated words only once.

combine.hint: Who attended the ceremony?
accepted: The principal and the parents attended the ceremony.
The parents and the principal attended the ceremony.

items.stem: Join the two sentences into one compound sentence. Use the joining word.

explanation.whyCorrect: Or joins two choices. Two complete sentences need a comma before or; one subject with two actions does not.
explanation.tip: Or shows a choice.

sentences: We can take the metro to the stadium.
combine.hint: What are the two ways to get to the stadium?
accepted: We can take the metro to the stadium, or we can walk there.
We can take the metro to the stadium or walk there.
